when: the years since the well was dug
what: The Imperials set the well's stone head and lining in the clay bank by the ford. The bank moves with every monsoon, and the stone cracks. Each dry season Livia Varinius re-mortars the cracks herself and says nothing of it aloud.
A new crack opens in the well head, a finger wide, on the side that faces the ford. Livia writes it in the station ledger in the old log's order (time, count, state), and tells nobody.

Ford water and fine silt come in through the crack. The morning bucket comes up with silt in the bottom, and the water tastes of the ford. Livia keeps the silt in a jar on the coping, to show a mason when one comes.
Livia asks the landing to haul stone for a new lining. Signs-For-The-Cargo refuses. The landing does not build in stone, and it does not drink the well's water.

Livia sets a charge of two drakes on every traveller who stops at the station, for the stop and its water, to pay a mason from Gideon to re-line the well in stone. She charges the landing's people nothing for water, as she always has.

when: a few days after t5, before 6 Rain's Hand
what: In answer, Signs-For-The-Cargo sets a charge of one drake a head on walkers who wade the ford, as well as the carts he takes across on the raft by the wheel. He says the ford was worked before the well was dug. Travellers ask Livia why they pay twice.
Some travellers who have paid at the station wade the ford at night below the raft, to dodge the landing's charge. The landing finds their prints in the clay at the bend at dawn.

A crocodile, drawn by the offal from the drying racks and the night waders, takes the deep water under the clay bend. It comes up at Signs-For-The-Cargo while he digs plaster clay. He drops the clay basket at the cut and runs. Nobody has dug there since, and the crocodile comes up at anyone on the cut, day or night.

The rains are about seven days off. The landing must replaster its walls before them and has no clay. Takes-The-Short-Weight, who judges everything by its water, tastes the ford in the well water when she draws for the brine she must not make with it. She thinks the landing's charge on walkers is wrong and sends waders to the bend, and does not say so to Signs-For-The-Cargo.
Ahzi-Tal, a Helstrom courier, lodges for one night. Reeh-Shaal, who pays for her bed in salt and travels the same road, sees that his satchel holds a sealed packet his ledger does not list.
Reeh-Shaal buys a length of rope from Tsono-Ra after the lodge has closed, saying she needs it to tie her pack.

Reeh-Shaal kills Ahzi-Tal at the stone lip, takes the satchel, ties the body's wrists and pins it with a grave-stake in the spring's throat under the Hist's roots, so it will not float up. She leaves the stake's face uncarved.
Haj-Tei finds the courier's bed empty, his pack still in the lodge store and his bill unpaid. He decides the courier left before dawn without paying and keeps the pack against the debt.
The body fouls the water. Guests who drink it, or eat food cooked in it, fall sick with fever and retching.
Reeh-Shaal stays at the lodge, saying she waits for a boat to Helstrom. She waits for the packet's buyer, who has not come, and tells the sick guests it is the fire stand's food.
After the lamps are out, Reeh-Shaal goes to the stone lip and looks down into the water for a while, to be sure the body has not come up.

In a dry year the founders went down the root galleries and cut a channel from a brine seam toward the roots of a rival grove downstream, to sour its water and take its travellers. The rival grove withered; Greenspring grew.
The founders carved the descent on their own grave-stakes in the old way, as a deed done for the tribe, and never spoke of it to outsiders.
With the grove downstream dead, the channel silted on that side; each flood now pushes the brine back up the cut into Greenspring's own taproots.
Vees-Wai finds the Hist's leaves falling out of season and the sap thin. The village tastes salt in the spring and blames the salt works upstream.
Ixo-Vaal stopped trading for salt-works salt when the works closed their landing; he now buys upriver rock salt, which he keeps in a sack at his door.
